assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum cascade laser is a clear invention: a unipolar intersubband laser whose emission wavelength is set by layer thicknesses rather than the bandgap, made possible by band-structure engineering and precisely controlled epitaxial growth. It opened the mid-infrared and terahertz ranges to compact sources and underpins gas sensing and spectroscopy. This is the kind of discovery or invention with a concrete device and broad downstream use that fits the prize criteria and my experience with layered semiconductor and interface materials.
assessment.attribution: The 1994 demonstration at Bell Labs is associated with Faist and Capasso, with Cho's molecular-beam-epitaxy growth essential to realizing the heterostructures. Others in the Bell Labs team and earlier proposals (e.g. Kazarinov and Suris) may deserve mention; I cannot confirm from the supplied text how much weight each deserves. Capasso, Faist and Cho form a defensible three-person configuration, with Cho's role being the one most open to debate.
assessment.maturity: Thirty years of room-temperature continuous-wave operation, commercial products and independent groups worldwide give very strong confirmation. Recognition is, if anything, overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the growth contribution (Cho) is judged decisive or enabling.
Prior theoretical proposals (Kazarinov and Suris) not among the credited names.
Whether the committee views this as applied engineering rather than physics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect introduced a new classification of electronic phases and a large experimental field, with edge and surface states that are directly measurable by transport and spectroscopy. The conceptual originality is high and the effect on materials physics is lasting.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical prediction for graphene; Molenkamp's group gave the first experimental observation in HgTe/CdTe wells following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the three-dimensional work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan are not in the credited names, so the configuration leaves out significant contributors. Splitting theory and experiment as proposed is reasonable but not complete.
assessment.maturity: Experimental confirmation in HgTe wells and in bismuth-based three-dimensional materials with ARPES is well established and independent. Over fifteen years have passed, so timing is appropriate.
uncertainties: Omitted contributors (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and others) in the credited-name constraint.
Whether the 2D quantum spin Hall effect or 3D topological insulators carry the central credit.
Relationship to the 2016 prize on topological phases.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a field of tunable correlated and superconducting states in moire materials. The idea that a twist angle can set the electronic bandwidth is original and the experiments show correlated insulators and superconductivity in a very simple material, with a large field following.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted flat bands at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero and colleagues observed the correlated insulator and superconductivity in 2018. This is a plausible theory plus experiment pairing. Other groups (e.g. Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov, Cao as first author) contributed important confirmations and extensions that are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by several independent groups and developed into fractional Chern insulator and related physics. Interpretation of the superconducting mechanism is still unsettled, and recognition could be considered somewhat early.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of the superconductivity remains debated.
Which later moire results belong to the same prize topic.
Sample-dependence and reproducibility details I cannot verify here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond created a room-temperature solid-state spin system that serves as a quantum sensor and qubit. The importance to nanoscale magnetic, electric and thermal sensing and to biology is substantial, and the platform links defect physics, optics and microscopy.
assessment.attribution: The first optical detection of single NV spins (Gruber et al., 1997) and coherent control (Jelezko, Wrachtrup and collaborators, 2004) point to Wrachtrup and Jelezko. Lukin's group contributed quantum registers and sensing demonstrations, but its decisive role in the original discovery is less clear from the supplied credit. Others, such as Awschalom, Hanson and Lukin's collaborators, also have strong claims; the allocation is open.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups reproduce and apply the method, and commercial sensors exist. Applications in quantum technology are still evolving, so a clear and bounded discovery needs to be defined.
uncertainties: Allocation among Wrachtrup, Jelezko, Lukin and others not credited.
Whether the prize topic is the single-spin control or the sensing applications.
Overlap with the separate optical spin-control candidate (optical control of solid-state spins).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: High-resolution angle-resolved photoemission turned a surface spectroscopy into a quantitative probe of band structure, gaps and many-body interactions in correlated materials, notably cuprate superconductors. The instrument and method development behind it changed how quantum materials are studied, and I regard this as a real methodological achievement.
assessment.attribution: Campuzano and Shen are named for early cuprate Fermi surface and gap measurements. The method was built from contributions of many groups, including detector and synchrotron-beamline developers and others such as Hufner, Dessau and Damascelli, so credit for the technique as a whole is diffuse and the pair is partial.
assessment.maturity: Widely confirmed and used for decades; the physical interpretation of cuprate results remains open, but the method itself is mature.
uncertainties: Diffuse credit for a technique built over many years.
Whether the prize would recognize method or particular cuprate findings.
Relationship to unresolved cuprate theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reproducible room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions was a breakthrough in spin-dependent transport and led to magnetic read heads and MRAM. The discovery depends on high-quality thin-film interfaces, which I appreciate as an interface microscopy specialist.
assessment.attribution: Moodera and Miyazaki reported large room-temperature TMR independently in 1995. Parkin's later MgO-based high TMR is important for applications, though is a separate step; Julliere's 1975 low-temperature result is not credited. The credit is reasonably clear for the 1995 result but depends on how the topic is framed.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed and commercialized. The 2007 prize for giant magnetoresistance covers a close relative, which makes the novelty argument harder.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2007 GMR prize.
Whether MgO coherent tunnelling (Parkin, Yuasa and others) should be treated as the same discovery.
Julliere's earlier work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of superconductivity in iron pnictides in 2008 opened a second family of high-temperature superconductors beyond the cuprates, with transition temperatures reaching above 50 K and a distinctive multiband electronic structure. It is original and clearly a discovery.
assessment.attribution: Hosono's group reported superconductivity in LaFeAsO(1-x)Fx; Chen and Zhao quickly raised the transition temperature in related compounds. A single laureate is supportable on originality, and adding Chen or Zhao would recognise follow-up improvements; the choice involves judgment I have not independently verified.
assessment.maturity: Broadly confirmed and a large field, though the pairing mechanism is not settled and no applications have yet arrived; recognition could be viewed as premature relative to the mechanism.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism unresolved.
Whether the improvements by Chen and Zhao deserve shared credit.
Limited practical impact so far.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, with the magic-wavelength idea of Katori, enabled atomic clocks of unprecedented stability and accuracy at the 10^-18 level, with consequences for metrology, tests of fundamental physics and geodesy. It is a clear invention with measurable performance.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and Ye led the realization of record-performance clocks; this pairing is natural. Others, notably Ludlow and Kimble contributions, are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Strong independent confirmation across several laboratories; a future redefinition of the second would reinforce impact. Timing is plausible, though the 2012 and 2005 prizes in related precision measurement may affect priority.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier prizes on laser frequency combs and ion clocks.
Whether practical clock redefinition should precede recognition.
Contributions by others not in the credited names.
